His dedication to his craft has attracted renowned talent like Yuri Lowenthal to collaborate with him on his projects. As he grows and improves, Eddie is a shining example of a self-starter.

No, nobody thinks that The Flash is a perfect show. However, there are some phenomenal episodes within its long, 9-season run—some can even be considered masterpieces. While, for the most part, the show was only considered masterful in its first few seasons, there are still a couple of Season 3 and onward episodes that are masterpieces.

Regardless of the season an episode originates from, these entries in The Flash saga are incredible in one way or another—or all of the ways, really—and are worth noting, even three years post-finale. The high-flying, fast-paced action and wonderful storytelling are nonstop... in these episodes, at least.

blocks.c: Oliver Queen as The Flash in The Flash Season 5, Episode 9

blocks.x: The CW "Arrowverse" loved doing crossover episodes, and as the universe grew and more characters got involved, they got to go bigger and bigger. One of the best came in the form of the "Elseworlds" event, spanning across The Flash, Arrow, and Supergirl—the first part airing on the Scarlet Speedster's show. The Flash Season 5, Episode 9, "Elseworlds, Part 1" is a great introduction episode for the crossover event, and has so much fun with the premise.

When Barry and Oliver Queen (Stephen Amell) wake up as each other—they keep their own bodies, but they're known as each other now—and the rest of the world believes they've been like that forever, something has clearly gone wrong, and they need to come together to figure it out. Supergirl (Melissa Benoist) gets involved, also being incredibly confused. Seeing this premise come to life, with great performances from the three protagonists, makes for such a fun episode.

blocks.c: Savitar about to stab Iris West in The Flash Season 3, Episode 22

blocks.x: The Flash Season 3, Episode 22, "Infantino Street" is a great, living and breathing example of why Season 3 is so much better than people have ever given it credit for. The way this 22nd entry in the season brings the culmination of the tension regarding Iris West's (Candice Patton) potential future death to a head is excellent.

Early on in Season 3, Barry Allen (Grant Gustin) sees a vision from the future that depicts the villain of the season, Savitar (Tobin Bell and Grant Gustin), murdering the love of his life in front of his future self. From that moment on, the conflict of the season became about how to prevent Iris from meeting her terrifying end. This episode is where it comes down to the final hour, and Barry must team up with Captain Cold (Wentworth Miller) to steal a piece of technology to save Iris on the night she's supposed to die.

blocks.c: Jay Garrick with a mask on in a prison cell, banging on it in The Flash Season 2, Episode 14

blocks.x: After such a successful first season, the team behind The Flash had to work super hard to make sure they didn't drop the ball on Season 2. With such high expectations from audiences, they decided they were going to jump into the world of the multiverse. With an all-new Harrison Wells—"Harry"—from a parallel Earth, it was only a matter of time before Team Flash themselves went to "Earth-2."

They finally do so in The Flash Season 2, Episode 13, "Welcome to Earth-2," but when things go awry, they need to leave in the episode directly after: The Flash Season 1, Episode 14, "Escape from Earth-2." There are some awesome multiversal doppelgänger interactions here, and the stakes are high as they discover more and more about Zoom (Tony Todd) and what the truth behind him might be.

blocks.c: Joe West and Barry Allen investigating Harrison Wells' true body in The Flash Season 1, Episode 19

blocks.x: The mystery of who Harrison Wells (Tom Cavanagh) truly is may be one of the best mysteries to watch unfold in this show. While the audience finds out who he really is in "The Man in the Yellow Suit," the Flash team doesn't. Barry and co. actually discover this secret in Season 1's "Who Is Harrison Wells?"—exactly ten episodes later.

Watching them as they get closer and closer to the truth, with Wells scheming in the background—adding tension that he will discover their investigation and strike—is so engaging. The tension is massive and intense, and that makes for a plot that is unforgettable, which is needed for such an important moment in the great superhero show.

blocks.c: Killer Frost scowling in The Flash Season 3, Episode 20

blocks.x: Despite the flak that Season 3 gets—especially the flak it got upon first release—it's far better than people give it credit for, especially in hindsight of the other seasons to come after. One of the best entries in Season 3 is, without a doubt, "I Know Who You Are." This is primarily because of the stellar emotional drama within it between the likes of Team Flash and their ride-or-die friend-turned-enemy, Caitlyn Snow (Danielle Panabaker), now known as Killer Frost.

The kind of emotional drama found within this episode makes it so compelling from start to finish. By this point in the series, Caitlyn has become family to not just the rest of Team Flash, but the audience, as well. So, when she goes bad, it's genuinely heartbreaking, especially when both Barry and the viewer can see the good still within her. The real highlight of this episode, though, is none other than the gigantic reveal of Savitar's identity... a temporal clone of Barry Allen himself.

blocks.c: Seasons 1 and 2 Barry Allen standing at a computer together in The Flash Season 2, Episode 17

blocks.x: Time travel has been important to the character of The Flash since the very beginning. This is true for the first season of the CW show, too. Barry is dead-set on determining the secret to upping his speed via the methods of his nemesis, Eobard Thawne, aka The Reverse Flash. However, this causes some serious problems, not just for Barry, but for all of his friends in the past timeline.

When he goes back, the speedster accidentally gains the attention of a Time Wraith, protectors of the timeline that have a nasty, ghostly figure. Watching as Barry tries to blend in and be his last self, while Eobard slowly figures out who he really is, is so entertaining and genuinely adds to the tension of the episode.

blocks.c: Grant Gustin, Stephen Amell, and Robbie Amell in The Flash

blocks.x: Penultimate episodes can be pretty hit or miss on television, and, boy, did The Flash find a hitter in Season 1's "Rogue Air." Barry tries to save the metahumans they've imprisoned in the Particle Accelerator over the course of the season when Eobard Thawne—disguised as Harrison Wells—decides to turn it on again. However, as per usual, the plan doesn't go the way he hoped.

It's the finale of this episode that really causes it to stand out, though, as it's the big battle against Reverse Flash, who is facing not just Flash, but Arrow and Firestorm (Robbie Amell), as well. This 3-v-1 fight is abundantly exciting and proves just how powerful Reverse Flash actually is, which adds to the stakes of the season finale to come.
